 * It owns a static framebuffer and drives an XLCDC hardware layer directly (the
 * same way video.c drives the camera on HEO), so it can be on screen before
 * Legato / the Marvin screen is built — the image lives in QSPI NOR
 * (flash/qspi_layout.h QSPI_SPLASH_OFFSET, provisioned with openocd/program-qspi.sh)
 * as raw RGBA8888 pixels in the layer's native byte order, so displaying it is a
 * flash read straight into the framebuffer the LCDC scans out: no JPEG decode, no
 * widgets, no Legato, no SD. Reading from QSPI keeps the SD bring-up out of the
 * splash path — splash up in ~260 ms, no card needed.
 *
 * ui_manager owns hardware-layer policy and passes the layer to show/hide on. */

/* Read the splash image from QSPI NOR into the framebuffer. Returns true if it
 * loaded; on a flash error the buffer is filled with an opaque fallback colour and
 * false is returned — either way the framebuffer is displayable. Uses the SST26
 * driver; call from a task once the scheduler is running. */
bool Splash_Load(void);

/* Program the given XLCDC layer to scan the splash framebuffer (full-screen,
 * opaque, RGBA8888) and enable it. */
void Splash_Show(XLCDC_LAYER layer);

void Splash_Hide(XLCDC_LAYER layer);

#endif /* UI_SCREEN_SPLASH_H */

Adopting the framework model makes "each panel owns its own canvas" literally true (define up to 8 layer-screens, composite any 3 onto the HW layers), aligns with the tooling instead of fighting it, deletes two standing hacks, and is purpose-built for marvin's need (multiple coexisting overlays with preserved widget state, no redraw on transition). Splash stays out of the master screen because it must paint before Legato/the master screen is built (fast-boot path). |  (`data/ui/make-splash.sh`), not by ad-hoc shell history; the raw byte order is `[A,B,G,R]` per pixel.** The XLCDC splash canvas is `GFX_COLOR_MODE_RGBA_8888` whose pixel word is `0xRRGGBBAA` (`splash.c` `SPLASH_FILL 0x000000FF` = opaque black confirms it), so little-endian memory bytes are `[A,B,G,R]` — **not** Pillow's default `R,G,B,A`. The script splits channels and `Image.merge("RGBA",(a,b,g,r))` to get that order, resizes to 1280×800, and asserts the 4,096,000-byte size `splash.c` requires. #include "ui/screens/dashboard/screen_dashboard.h"

#include "ui/ui_manager.h"   /* CANVAS_DASH, BASE_W, BASE_H */

#include "gfx/canvas/gfx_canvas_api.h"

/* Dashboard surface, non-cached so the 2D engine and LCDC DMA read CPU-rendered
 * pixels coherently; 32-byte aligned. RGB565 — steady-state UI needs no more. */
#define FB_NOCACHE   __attribute__((section(".region_nocache"), aligned (32)))

static uint16_t FB_NOCACHE s_fb[BASE_W * BASE_H];

void Dash_InitSurface(void)
{
    gfxcSetPixelBuffer(CANVAS_DASH, BASE_W, BASE_H, GFX_COLOR_MODE_RGB_565, s_fb);
}

void Dash_Setup(void)
{
    /* Full-screen at the origin. The root is on Legato layer 0 (built by MGS); the
     * canvas window positions that layer's pixels on the display. */
    gfxcSetWindowPosition(CANVAS_DASH, 0, 0);
    gfxcSetWindowSize(CANVAS_DASH, BASE_W, BASE_H);
}

#include "ui/screens/navigation/screen_navigation.h"

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdint.h>

#include "ui/ui_manager.h"   /* CANVAS_NAVIGATION */
#include "ui/widgets/button_aa/widget_button_aa.h"

#include "gfx/canvas/gfx_canvas_api.h"
#include "gfx/legato/legato.h"
#include "gfx/legato/generated/le_gen_scheme.h"
#include "gfx/legato/generated/screen/le_gen_screen_Marvin.h"   /* nav widgets + hamburger event */

/* The navigation drawer is layer 1 of the Marvin master screen, rendered into its
 * own canvas (CANVAS_NAVIGATION, defined in ui_manager.h). It is layer-agnostic —
 * ui_manager (the compositor) decides which hardware layer this canvas is shown
 * on; the drawer's slide works on the canvas window, independent of the layer. */
#define NAVIGATION_W   320u
#define NAVIGATION_H   800u

/* gfxcStartEffectMove delta — slide feel (DEC = ease-out). Tune to taste. */
#define NAVIGATION_SLIDE_DELTA  6u

/* Off-screen-left X for the closed drawer / slide-out target.
 *
 * A canvas layer can't truly sit off-screen — the window-clip (gfx_canvas.c
 * _gfxcCanvasUpdate) emulates a negative X by shifting the source pointer right
 * and shrinking the window. But it first aligns X *down* to a multiple of
 * CANVAS_WIN_X_ALIGN (`x &= ~0x3` for non-32bpp surfaces), and once |X| reaches
 * the surface width the shifted pointer wraps to the next row, flashing the
 * panel's left columns through. So the furthest the drawer can validly sit is
 * the largest aligned X with |X| < NAVIGATION_W. We slide to there; navigation_fx_done
 * then disables the layer, clearing the residual edge sliver. Derived from
 * NAVIGATION_W so it tracks the surface width, not a hard-coded pixel count. */
#define CANVAS_WIN_X_ALIGN  4u   /* mirrors the clip's `x &= ~0x3` */
#define NAVIGATION_CLOSED_X (-(int)((NAVIGATION_W - 1u) & ~(CANVAS_WIN_X_ALIGN - 1u)))

/* Rounded button corners. The widget cornerRadius is honored by the classic
 * skin's background draw but isn't exposed in MGS, so we set it in code. */
#define NAVIGATION_CORNER_RADIUS  12u

#define FB_NOCACHE   __attribute__((section(".region_nocache"), aligned (32)))

static uint16_t FB_NOCACHE s_fb_navigation[NAVIGATION_W * NAVIGATION_H];

static bool s_navigation_open = false;

/* Navigation entries, in panel order. The selected one is the active screen. */
#define NAVIGATION_COUNT  6u

static leButtonWidget *navigation_button(unsigned int i)
{
    switch (i)
    {
        case 0:  return Marvin_BUTTON_NAV_DASHBOARD_0;
        case 1:  return Marvin_BUTTON_NAV_LOGS_0;
        case 2:  return Marvin_BUTTON_NAV_PERFORMANCE_0;
        case 3:  return Marvin_BUTTON_NAV_SYSTEM_INFO_0;
        case 4:  return Marvin_BUTTON_NAV_DIAGNOSTICS_0;
        default: return Marvin_BUTTON_NAV_SETTINGS_0;
    }
}

static void navigation_close(void);   /* forward decl — navigation_on_release may close the drawer */

/* Single-active highlight: paint the active entry selected, the rest unselected. */
static void navigation_highlight(leButtonWidget *active)
{
    unsigned int i;

    for (i = 0u; i < NAVIGATION_COUNT; i++)
    {
        leButtonWidget *b = navigation_button(i);
        b->fn->setScheme(b, (b == active) ? &SCHEME_NAV_BUTTON_SELECTED
                                          : &SCHEME_NAV_BUTTON_UNSELECTED);
    }
}

/* Released-event sink for every navigation entry. Switch the highlight; Dashboard
 * means "back to the main view" so it also closes the drawer, while the other
 * entries just change the selection and stay open. The active screen-switch will
 * hook here once the per-screen canvas model lands. */
static void navigation_on_release(leButtonWidget *btn)
{
    navigation_highlight(btn);

    if (btn == Marvin_BUTTON_NAV_DASHBOARD_0)
    {
        navigation_close();
    }
}

static void navigation_buttons_init(void)
{
    unsigned int i;

    /* Route every navigation-entry release through navigation_on_release
     * (runtime-registered here — the screen wires no button events itself) and
     * round the corners (not an MGS option). */
    for (i = 0u; i < NAVIGATION_COUNT; i++)
    {
        navigation_button(i)->fn->setReleasedEventCallback(navigation_button(i), navigation_on_release);
        navigation_button(i)->fn->setCornerRadius(navigation_button(i), NAVIGATION_CORNER_RADIUS);
        ButtonAA_Enable(navigation_button(i));
    }

    /* Dashboard is the active entry at startup — set the highlight only (calling
     * the release sink here would close the not-yet-open drawer). */
    navigation_highlight(Marvin_BUTTON_NAV_DASHBOARD_0);
}

/* Animate the drawer to target_x from wherever it currently sits. Cancel any
 * in-flight slide first: gfxcStartEffectMove is a no-op while a move is running
 * (it only starts from status IDLE), so without the stop a mid-slide reversal
 * would be silently dropped — the original move would run to completion and fire
 * navigation_fx_done with a now-stale s_navigation_open, hiding the drawer and
 * wedging the toggle. Reading the live position makes the reversal retarget smoothly. */
static void navigation_slide_to(int target_x)
{
    int x, y;

    gfxcStopEffect(CANVAS_NAVIGATION, GFXC_FX_MOVE);
    gfxcGetWindowPosition(CANVAS_NAVIGATION, &x, &y);
    gfxcStartEffectMove(CANVAS_NAVIGATION, GFXC_FX_MOVE_DEC, x, 0, target_x, 0, NAVIGATION_SLIDE_DELTA);
}

static void navigation_open(void)
{
    /* Force a full repaint of the panel into the canvas before revealing it — the
     * paint queued at startup (parked off-screen) doesn't fully land in the
     * buffer, so without this the drawer slides in partially drawn until touch
     * damage fills it in. The repaint lands over the next frames as it slides.
     * Show first so the move is visible (the FX engine enables the layer from
     * canvas.active). */
    Marvin_PANEL_NAVIGATION->fn->invalidate(Marvin_PANEL_NAVIGATION);
    gfxcShowCanvas(CANVAS_NAVIGATION);
    navigation_slide_to(0);
    s_navigation_open = true;
}

static void navigation_close(void)
{
    /* Slide out to NAVIGATION_CLOSED_X (off-screen), then navigation_fx_done
     * disables the layer. NAVIGATION_CLOSED_X avoids the -NAVIGATION_W window-clip
     * row-wrap (see its definition); the layer update busy-waits for the vsync latch,
     * so the final frame is displayed before the hide lands — keeping it in-bounds
     * makes that frame a harmless edge sliver instead of the panel's left columns. */
    navigation_slide_to(NAVIGATION_CLOSED_X);
    s_navigation_open = false;
}

/* Move-effect completion callback. At the off-screen end of a close slide the
 * window clip leaves a degenerate sliver of the drawer composited at screen
 * left; hiding the canvas (disabling its layer) once the slide finishes removes it cleanly. Only
 * acts on a completed close — an open leaves the layer shown, and a re-open
 * mid-close restarts the move (so this won't fire for the abandoned close). */
static void navigation_fx_done(unsigned int canvasID, GFXC_FX_TYPE effect,
                               GFXC_FX_STATUS status, void *parm)
{
    (void)canvasID;
    (void)parm;

    if (effect == GFXC_FX_MOVE && status == GFXC_FX_DONE && !s_navigation_open)
    {
        gfxcHideCanvas(CANVAS_NAVIGATION);
        gfxcCanvasUpdate(CANVAS_NAVIGATION);
    }
}

void Navigation_InitSurface(void)
{
    gfxcSetPixelBuffer(CANVAS_NAVIGATION, NAVIGATION_W, NAVIGATION_H, GFX_COLOR_MODE_RGB_565, s_fb_navigation);
}

/* Per-panel setup for the navigation drawer (Marvin layer-screen 1,
 * CANVAS_NAVIGATION). MGS has already built the panel onto Legato layer 1; here we
 * set the canvas window (parked off-screen / closed), the move-FX callback, and
 * wire the buttons. The canvas is bound to a hardware layer by ui_manager. Keep the
 * panel visible+enabled so Legato renders it continuously, and start closed: the
 * touch pick rect follows the canvas window position (LE_DRIVER_LAYER_MODE), so a
 * closed (off-screen) drawer can't intercept dashboard touches, and the off-screen
 * X seeds the slide-in. */
void Navigation_Setup(void)
{
    Marvin_PANEL_NAVIGATION->fn->setEnabled(Marvin_PANEL_NAVIGATION, LE_TRUE);
    Marvin_PANEL_NAVIGATION->fn->setVisible(Marvin_PANEL_NAVIGATION, LE_TRUE);

    gfxcSetWindowSize(CANVAS_NAVIGATION, NAVIGATION_W, NAVIGATION_H);
    gfxcSetWindowPosition(CANVAS_NAVIGATION, NAVIGATION_CLOSED_X, 0);
    gfxcSetEffectsCallback(CANVAS_NAVIGATION, navigation_fx_done, NULL);

    navigation_buttons_init();
}

/* Hamburger on the dashboard (BASE) toggles the navigation drawer. */
void event_Marvin_BUTTON_SYSYEM_NAVIGATION_OnPressed(leButtonWidget* btn)
{
    (void)btn;
    if (s_navigation_open) { navigation_close(); } else { navigation_open(); }
}

docs/journal.md:36:| 2026-06-29 | **Migrate the operator UI to MGS's single-master-screen / layer-screen model: one master Legato screen `Marvin` whose *layers* are the panels (dashboard, nav, song-select, dialogs…), replacing the current "separate 1-layer MGS Screen per panel, manually re-hosted by `ui_manager`, `LE_LAYER_COUNT` pinned by a fake `LayerBudget` screen."** Per Microchip's GFX-canvas **layer-screen** guide, this is the framework's intended structure: MGS derives `LE_LAYER_COUNT` from the layer count and auto-associates each layer-screen with its own GFX canvas, so the `LayerBudget` pin, the `compat/le_gen_init.h` stub, and the `init_screens()` build-on-layer-0-then-disconnect + per-screen `*_OnShow` re-host dance all disappear. `ui_manager` shrinks to: assign each layer-screen's canvas buffer (content-sized, RGB565) + `show_layer(idx, hwLayer)` / `hide_layer(idx)` verbs (HW-layer binding stays a runtime `gfxcSetLayer` choice, never owned by a panel). Panel modules (`screen_nav.c`, `screen_song_select.c`, …) keep content + event wiring + interaction FX but drop all `leAddRootWidget`/canvas mechanics. **Splash stays separate/manual** (pre-Legato RGBA8888 scanout) on a canvas slot *outside* the layer-screen range 0..N-1 (e.g. top of the 8-slot pool). The three-concept model that drove this (Legato layer-screen ↔ canvas coupled 1:1; XLCDC HW layer independent/runtime) + the direction are now canonical in [`ui_compositor.md`](ui_compositor.md) §0. Open items before coding: final layer order/z-order + initial layer set; per-layer-screen canvas sizing/offset; MGS widget naming across layers (drives a rename sweep in the panel modules); confirm a hidden layer-screen's canvas suppresses touch picking. | The current approach hand-emulates layer-screens, which is what forced every recurring canvas-vs-layer confusion: with `LE_LAYER_COUNT`=3 only canvases 0/1/2 are real Legato render targets, so a 3rd live panel could not get its own slot without colliding with the splash's. Adopting the framework model makes "each panel owns its own canvas" literally true (define up to 8 layer-screens, composite any 3 onto the HW layers), aligns with the tooling instead of fighting it, deletes two standing hacks, and is purpose-built for marvin's need (multiple coexisting overlays with preserved widget state, no redraw on transition). Splash stays out of the master screen because it must paint before Legato/the master screen is built (fast-boot path). |  (`data/ui/make-splash.sh`), not by ad-hoc shell history; the raw byte order is `[A,B,G,R]` per pixel.** The XLCDC splash canvas is `GFX_COLOR_MODE_RGBA_8888` whose pixel word is `0xRRGGBBAA` (`splash.c` `SPLASH_FILL 0x000000FF` = opaque black confirms it), so little-endian memory bytes are `[A,B,G,R]` — **not** Pillow's default `R,G,B,A`. The script splits channels and `Image.merge("RGBA",(a,b,g,r))` to get that order, resizes to 1280×800, and asserts the 4,096,000-byte size `splash.c` requires. Uses `uv` + Pillow (no ImageMagick/ffmpeg — neither is installed on this host). Verified empirically against the committed `splash.raw`: first pixel matched to within JPEG-re-encode noise, while the naive `R,G,B,A` ordering was fully reversed. Regenerated `splash.raw` from the (newer) `splash.jpg`, which had drifted out of sync. Documented in `data/README.md`; flash with `openocd/program-qspi.sh splash`. | The conversion step previously lived only in someone's shell history — undocumented and reproducible only by guessing the byte order (easy to get reversed, since the framework name "RGBA_8888" reads like Pillow's `R,G,B,A` but the little-endian word layout inverts it). A checked-in script with the size assertion makes the splash pipeline self-serve and drift-proof, and pairs with the existing `program-qspi.sh splash` provisioning step. |
docs/journal.md:223:`bind_canvas(CANVAS_NAV, OVR1)` reprograms OVR1 from scratch. `ui_manager` deleted `CANVAS_SPLASH`
docs/journal.md:233:Code side: `ui_manager` no longer builds/disconnects/re-hosts per screen — it calls `screenInit_Marvin()` once, then per-panel `Nav_Setup()`/`SongSel_Setup()` (window + event wiring on already-placed widgets), and binds canvases to HW layers at display time. New `ui/screens/song_select/screen_song_select.c` (owns CANVAS_SONGSEL=2, content-sized RGB565 buffer, centered window at (90,70)). `screen_nav.c` ported to `Marvin_*_0` widgets, re-host dropped, `Navigation_OnShow`→`Nav_Setup`. `manual_input.c` strum handlers renamed. **Splash moved off canvas slot 2 → slot 7** (outside the layer-screen range 0..2, since L2 now renders into canvas[2]). Retired `widget_song_list_demo` + its `songlist` console command (its job was bring-up before a real song-select screen existed). At reveal the song-select dialog is brought up on OVR2 over the live dashboard — the initial "on screen at startup" milestone. Builds clean (xc32 v5.10) and **boots on hardware** — splash → dashboard with the song-select dialog centered on OVR2 over the live dashboard.
docs/journal.md:235:**Gotcha that cost a debug round (silent prefetch-abort, splash never revealed):** for the regenerated Marvin screen, `screenInit_Marvin` only flips the one-time `initialized` flag — the **widget tree is constructed in `screenShow_Marvin`** (the `leWidget_New` calls + `leAddRootWidget(rootN, N)` + `leSetLayerColorMode`). Calling only `screenInit_Marvin()` built nothing, so every widget global stayed NULL and `Nav_Setup`'s first `widget->fn->...` call dereferenced NULL → `prefetch_abort` to PC `0x60` (fault handlers are silent `while(1)` spins, so it just froze with the log stuck mid-line). Fix: `ui_manager` calls `screenInit_Marvin()` **then `screenShow_Marvin()`**. (So the earlier "only `screenInit` + `screenGetRoot` needed" was wrong — `screenShow_` does the construction.) Diagnosed by dumping the widget pointers over the console (all `(nil)`) after marker-bisecting the boot task to between "marvin built" and "nav setup".
docs/journal.md:292:**Layer assignment is now ui_manager policy, never screen-owned.** `bind_canvas(canvas, hw, mode, show)` is the one place a canvas meets a layer; it pokes the layer's RGBMODE to match the canvas (the XLCDC driver never writes it), so the old "restore OVR1→RGB565 for nav" special case is gone. Splash holds OVR1 during boot; nav is bound to OVR1 only at reveal (after the splash vacates it — never shared live). `screen_nav.c`: dropped the hardcoded `gfxcSetLayer(NAV_CANVAS, HW_OVR1)` and local `HW_OVR1`/`NAV_CANVAS` (now `CANVAS_NAV` from `ui_manager.h`); `Navigation_OnShow` is the layer-agnostic host hook. (Memory `marvin-canvas-layer-binding` strengthened — Greg corrected this repeatedly.)
docs/journal.md:419:- **Terminology cleanup** across `ui/`: a *canvas* is the Legato render surface; a *hardware layer* is the LCDC scanout; they're bound at runtime and their indices are unrelated. Renamed `screen_nav.c` `NAV_LAYER` → `NAV_CANVAS` and rewrote all comments that called canvases "Legato layers" (ui_manager, screen_nav.{c,h}, screen_splash.h, loader). (Greg flags `NAV_CANVAS` naming + having a higher level assign the canvas→layer binding on show as a future refactor.)
docs/journal.md:474:- `screens/<name>/screen_<name>.{c,h}` — one folder per panel. Today: `screens/nav/screen_nav.{c,h}`.
docs/journal.md:477:`git mv` preserved history; updated all `#include "ui/…"` paths (include root is `default/src`, so they're now e.g. `ui/screens/nav/screen_nav.h`), include guards, the `user.cmake` source list, and `app.c`/`console.c` includers. C API symbol names (`Nav_*`, `SongList_*`, `ButtonAA_*`) left unchanged. Convention going forward: a new screen adds a `screens/<name>/` folder, a new widget a `widgets/<name>/` folder, each wired into `user.cmake`.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-30 00:56:41Z)**_

Good instinct — and yes, let's match the camelCase the rest of the codebase uses (`UiManager_Initialize`, `ButtonAA_Enable`, `SongList_New` are all `PascalModule_Method`). The cleanest fit with the `screen_<name>` file convention is a **`Screen<Name>_Method`** prefix — the symbol is just the PascalCase of the file's basename:

| Module file | Current | Proposed |
|---|---|---|
| `screen_dashboard` | `Dash_InitSurface` / `Dash_Setup` | `ScreenDashboard_InitSurface` / `ScreenDashboard_Setup` |
| `screen_navigation` | `Navigation_InitSurface` / `Navigation_Setup` | `ScreenNavigation_InitSurface` / `ScreenNavigation_Setup` |
| `screen_song_select` | `SongSel_InitSurface` / `SongSel_Setup` | `ScreenSongSelect_InitSurface` / `ScreenSongSelect_Setup` |
| `screen_splash` | `Splash_Load` / `Splash_Show` / `Splash_Hide` | `ScreenSplash_Load` / `ScreenSplash_Show` / `ScreenSplash_Hide` |

Why I'd go with `Screen<Name>_` over bare `Splash_`/`Dashboard_`:
- **Ties symbol to file** — `screen_splash.c` ↔ `ScreenSplash_*`, zero guessing.
- **Disambiguates from MGS** — generated entry points are lowercase `screenInit_Marvin` / `event_Marvin_*`; our PascalCase `ScreenSplash_*` won't be confused with them.
- **Kills the abbreviations** — `Dash`/`SongSel` were the inconsistent ones; this makes all four uniform and explicit (your stated goal).

The only cost is verbosity (`ScreenSongSelect_InitSurface` is long), but it's explicit and consistent, which is what you're after.

Scope note: I'd apply this to the **screen modules** only for now. The reusable widgets (`SongList_*`, `ButtonAA_*`) already read fine as widget APIs; if you want symmetry there too it'd be `Widget<Name>_*`, but `SongList_*` is referenced more widely so I'd treat that as a separate optional pass.

Want me to apply `Screen<Name>_*` across the four modules + their `ui_manager` call sites, and fold it into the same module-cleanup commit?

221	calls these — the modules never bind HW layers themselves. Headers are included from the
222	`default/src` root, e.g. `#include "ui/screens/navigation/screen_navigation.h"`. New panels add a

=== new le_gen_init.c ===
#include "gfx/legato/generated/le_gen_init.h"

static int32_t currentScreen;
static int32_t changingToScreen;

void legato_initializeScreenState(void)
{
    leSetStringTable(&stringTable);

    initializeStrings();

    screenInit_Marvin();

    currentScreen = -1;
    changingToScreen = -1;

    legato_showScreen(screenID_Marvin);
}

uint32_t legato_getCurrentScreen(void)
{
    return currentScreen;
}

static void legato_hideCurrentScreen(void)
{
    switch(currentScreen)
    {
        case screenID_Marvin:
        {
            screenHide_Marvin();
            currentScreen = 0;
            break;
        }
    }
}

void legato_showScreen(uint32_t id)
{
    if(changingToScreen >= 0)
        return;

    changingToScreen = id;
}

void legato_updateScreenState(void)
{
    if(leIsDrawing() == LE_TRUE)
        return;

    if(changingToScreen >= 0)
    {
        legato_hideCurrentScreen();

        leEvent_ClearList();

        switch(changingToScreen)
        {
            case screenID_Marvin:
            {
                screenShow_Marvin();
                break;
            }
        }

        currentScreen = changingToScreen;
        changingToScreen = -1;
    }

    switch(currentScreen)
    {
        case screenID_Marvin:
        {
            screenUpdate_Marvin();
            break;
        }
    }
}

leBool legato_isChangingScreens(void)
{
    return changingToScreen != -1;
}

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-30 01:10:22Z)**_

Here's my assessment — and the answer splits into "does it work?" and "is it worth it?"

## Does the state machine work with our model? Functionally, yes.
With one master `Marvin` screen, the state machine has exactly **one** screen. The thing that made it incompatible before — it shows one screen at a time and tears down the outgoing one on a switch — never triggers, because we never switch *screens*; we switch *layers* (canvas show/hide), which the state machine doesn't touch. So `legato_updateScreenState()` just builds+shows Marvin once and then calls `screenUpdate_Marvin()` every tick forever (harmless — it re-sets the three root sizes).

## But it doesn't buy us anything functional, and the current staged state isn't clean
Two real problems with where it sits right now:

1. **It's a second mechanism doing what `ui_manager` already does.** `le_gen_harmony.c` now auto-calls `legato_initializeScreenState()` (line 55, in `LEGATO_Initialize`) and `legato_updateScreenState()` (line 81, in `LEGATO_Tasks`). So the state machine will call `screenInit_Marvin()` + `screenShow_Marvin()` **on its own**, at an uncontrolled early time — while our boot task *also* calls them explicitly (guarded, splash-coordinated). The `showing` guard stops a double-build, but now the screen gets built by whoever wins the race, *not* in our deliberate splash→build→render-idle→reveal sequence.

2. **The compat stub now collides.** `default/src/compat/gfx/legato/generated/le_gen_init.h` still exists (on the include path via `user.cmake:43`) alongside the real generated `le_gen_init.h`. Two headers satisfy the same include; the stub doesn't even declare `legato_initializeScreenState`. That's a latent shadowing hazard that shouldn't ship.

To *cleanly adopt* the state machine we'd have to: delete the compat stub + its include path, **stop building the screen in `ui_manager`** and let the state machine own it, then rework the boot task to wait for `legato_getCurrentScreen() == screenID_Marvin` before running the `*_Setup()` wiring and the reveal. That's a non-trivial rework of the **most delicate, most-iterated part of the system** (the splash/boot timing), for zero new capability.

## Recommendation: back it out
The only upside is "stock MGS default + no compat stub" — a maintenance nicety, not a feature. Against that is reworking and re-testing the boot sequence with real regression risk. We don't switch screens, so the state machine is dead weight here.

If the recurring footgun of *remembering to disable it on every regen* is what's bugging you, that's the one argument for adopting it — but I'd say the compat stub (which is self-documenting and regen-stable) is the cheaper price.

So: I'd **re-disable "Generate Screen State Machine"** and keep the compat stub. Want me to hold while you flip it back in MGS and regen, then I'll re-review the staged diff to confirm we're back to the clean state? Or if you'd rather commit to adopting it, I'll scope the boot-task rework properly first.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-30 01:18:10Z)**_

Exactly as you suspected — the diff is minimal and surgical:

```c
// Application delta time query interface
uint32_t app_Legato_QueryDeltaTime(void);   // app MUST define this
...
-   leUpdate(0);
+   leUpdate(app_Legato_QueryDeltaTime());
```

So it swaps the hardcoded `leUpdate(0)` for `leUpdate(app_Legato_QueryDeltaTime())` and makes the app responsible for returning ms-since-last-update.

## Does it help our effects? No.
That `dt` feeds **Legato's own** time-based machinery — `leTimer`, Legato widget animations, built-in widget transitions/easing. **Our nav slide is GFX_CANVAS Move FX** (`gfxcStartEffectMove`), stepped by the canvas framework's own FX tick (`GFX_CANVAS_Task`, `NAVIGATION_SLIDE_DELTA` pixels/step) — completely independent of `leUpdate`'s `dt`. The proof: the slide already works today with `leUpdate(0)`. So delta-time changes nothing for the effects we have.

It would only matter if/when we adopt a **Legato-native** timed feature — a `leTimer`, a blinking caret, a Legato widget animation, etc. We use none of those right now.

## Cost of leaving it on
It's not free: with the interface enabled you **must** define `app_Legato_QueryDeltaTime()` somewhere or the link breaks (undefined symbol). So keeping it staged commits us to writing that hook now, for a capability we don't use.

## Recommendation: back it out (same call as the state machine)
Zero current benefit, and it forces an app hook. Re-enable it the day we actually use a Legato timer/animation — at which point the hook is ~5 lines (delta from `xTaskGetTickCount()`/`SYS_TIME`).

That said, this one's milder than the state machine — if you'd rather keep stock-MGS and be forward-looking, I can write a correct `app_Legato_QueryDeltaTime()` (FreeRTOS-tick delta) in ~5 lines and it'll sit there harmlessly until something needs it. Your call:
- **Disable** (my lean) — `leUpdate(0)` is fine for canvas-FX-only animation, and
- **Keep + I write the hook** — if you want real frame-time available for future Legato animations.

50	static void blend_corner(int32_t ox, int32_t oy,
51	                         leColor fill, leColorMode mode,
52	                         leBool flip_x, leBool flip_y)
53	{

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-30 01:35:29Z)**_

Here's the full picture and my assessment.

## What the buttons actually are
- **Difficulty + mode**: `LE_WIDGET_BORDER_LINE` → the classic skin draws a **1px rounded line border in the scheme's `SHADOWDARK` color** (`leWidget_SkinClassic_DrawRoundCornerLineBorder`), with a stepped arc at the corners.
- **SELECT**: `LE_WIDGET_BORDER_NONE` → no border, so the current fill-only AA already works on it. It's only the bordered ones that look wrong: today's AA blends *fill* over the corner and ignores the border line, so the stepped `SHADOWDARK` arc shows through / gets half-painted.

## "How hard is AA at runtime?" — it's cheap, and your premise is the key
`aa_paint` only runs when Legato repaints the widget, which only happens on **damage = a state change** (select/unselect/press). The screen is otherwise static (pre-rendered). So the AA cost is paid a handful of times per user tap, never per-frame. Even a fully analytic per-pixel corner (4 corners × R² px × a `sqrtf` each — ~576 px at R=12) is tens of µs, once, on a press. **So we can afford a richer, correct AA computed at runtime — no steady-state cost.** Your instinct is right.

## The extension is clean
Instead of "blend fill into the transition band," repaint each corner box with a **3-zone analytic blend** from the corner-center distance `d`:
- `d > R` → backdrop
- `R-1 < d < R` → AA backdrop↔border
- between → border (`SHADOWDARK`)
- `R-2 < d < R-1` → AA border↔fill
- inside → fill

i.e. two arc thresholds (`R` and `R − borderWidth`). Borderless buttons collapse to the current 2-zone (backdrop↔fill). Border color comes straight from `leScheme_GetRenderColor(scheme, LE_SCHM_SHADOWDARK)`; width is 1px for `LINE`.

## Variable radius — yes, do it at the same time
Drop the precomputed fixed mask and compute coverage per-pixel from `btn->widget.style.cornerRadius`. That removes the `BUTTON_AA_RADIUS == 12` constraint entirely — callers just `setCornerRadius(n)` + `ButtonAA_Enable`, any radius. (Optimization if ever needed: only `sqrtf` in the ~2px transition band, compare `d²` elsewhere — but unnecessary given it's on-change-only.)

## Plan / blast radius
- Rewrite the guts of `widget_button_aa.c`: analytic coverage (variable R), read `borderType` + `SHADOWDARK` border color, 2- or 3-zone blend, repaint the full corner box (erases the skin's stepped arc).
- API stays `ButtonAA_Enable(btn)` (now also reads radius + border). `BUTTON_AA_RADIUS` becomes an optional default constant rather than a hard requirement.
- **Nav is unaffected** (radius 12, no border → identical look). The song-select bordered buttons gain smooth border+fill corners.

Net: moderate, self-contained to one file, and the runtime cost is a non-issue. I'd go for it — border support **and** variable radius together. Want me to implement it?

#ifndef UI_GFX_AA_CORNERS_H
#define UI_GFX_AA_CORNERS_H

#include "gfx/legato/legato.h"   /* leRect, leColor, leColorMode */

#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif

/* Anti-alias the four rounded corners of a rect that a classic skin just drew with
 * a stepped arc. For each corner it repaints a radius×radius box: the backdrop
 * outside the arc (sampled once from the box's outer pixel — assumes a solid
 * backdrop behind the corner, true for our panels), an optional borderWidth-px
 * ring in `border`, then `fill` inside, with 1px anti-aliased bands at the arc
 * edges. borderWidth 0 → no border (backdrop↔fill).
 *
 * Coverage is computed analytically per pixel, so `radius` is arbitrary (bounded
 * by half the rect's smaller side). `mode` is the active render colour mode
 * (leRenderer_CurrentColorMode()). Call from a widget's paint override after the
 * normal draw; it only touches the corner boxes, so the straight edges the skin
 * drew (and any centred text) are left intact. Cheap, and runs only when the
 * widget repaints (state change) — not per frame.
 *
 * Widget-agnostic: the caller extracts fill/border/radius from its own widget +
 * scheme (see widget_button_aa.c). */
void AaCorners_Render(const leRect *rect, uint32_t radius, uint32_t borderWidth,
                      leColor fill, leColor border, leColorMode mode);

#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif

#endif /* UI_GFX_AA_CORNERS_H */

#include "ui/gfx/aa_corners.h"

#include <math.h>

#include "gfx/legato/common/legato_color.h"
#include "gfx/legato/renderer/legato_renderer.h"

/* Repaint one radius×radius corner box. (ox, oy) is its top-left in screen space;
 * (flip_x, flip_y) orient the arc centre so all four corners reuse the upper-left
 * math (centre at the box's inner corner). bg is sampled from the box's outer
 * pixel — the pixel furthest from the arc centre, which is always backdrop. Each
 * pixel is a blend of backdrop → border → fill by its coverage of the outer arc
 * (radius r) and inner arc (radius r-borderWidth). */
static void blend_corner(int32_t ox, int32_t oy, uint32_t r, uint32_t bw,
                         leColor fill, leColor border, leColorMode mode,
                         leBool flip_x, leBool flip_y)
{
    leColor   bg = leRenderer_GetPixel(flip_x ? ox + (int32_t)r - 1 : ox,
                                       flip_y ? oy + (int32_t)r - 1 : oy);
    uint32_t  px, py;

    for (py = 0u; py < r; py++)
    {
        for (px = 0u; px < r; px++)
        {
            uint32_t mx = flip_x ? (r - 1u - px) : px;
            uint32_t my = flip_y ? (r - 1u - py) : py;
            float    dx = (float)r - (float)mx - 0.5f;
            float    dy = (float)r - (float)my - 0.5f;
            float    d  = sqrtf(dx * dx + dy * dy);
            leColor  c;

            float co = (float)r + 0.5f - d;   /* coverage inside the outer arc */
            if (co < 0.0f) { co = 0.0f; } else if (co > 1.0f) { co = 1.0f; }

            if (bw == 0u)
            {
                c = leColorLerp(bg, fill, (uint32_t)(co * 100.0f + 0.5f), mode);
            }
            else
            {
                float ci = (float)(r - bw) + 0.5f - d;   /* coverage inside the fill */
                if (ci < 0.0f) { ci = 0.0f; } else if (ci > 1.0f) { ci = 1.0f; }

                c = leColorLerp(bg, border, (uint32_t)(co * 100.0f + 0.5f), mode);
                c = leColorLerp(c,  fill,   (uint32_t)(ci * 100.0f + 0.5f), mode);
            }

            leRenderer_PutPixel(ox + (int32_t)px, oy + (int32_t)py, c);
        }
    }
}

void AaCorners_Render(const leRect *rect, uint32_t radius, uint32_t borderWidth,
                      leColor fill, leColor border, leColorMode mode)
{
    int32_t r = (int32_t)radius;

    if (radius == 0u) { return; }

    blend_corner(rect->x,                       rect->y,                        radius, borderWidth, fill, border, mode, LE_FALSE, LE_FALSE);
    blend_corner(rect->x + rect->width - r,     rect->y,                        radius, borderWidth, fill, border, mode, LE_TRUE,  LE_FALSE);
    blend_corner(rect->x,                       rect->y + rect->height - r,     radius, borderWidth, fill, border, mode, LE_FALSE, LE_TRUE);
    blend_corner(rect->x + rect->width - r,     rect->y + rect->height - r,     radius, borderWidth, fill, border, mode, LE_TRUE,  LE_TRUE);
}

```

#include "ui/widgets/button_aa/widget_button_aa.h"

#include "ui/gfx/aa_corners.h"

#include "gfx/legato/core/legato_scheme.h"
#include "gfx/legato/renderer/legato_renderer.h"
#include "gfx/legato/widget/legato_widget.h"

/* One shared vtable copy + the captured original paint: every button shares the
 * same classic-skin vtable, so a single overridden copy serves all callers. */
static leButtonWidgetVTable s_aa_vt;
static void (*s_orig_paint)(leButtonWidget*);
static leBool s_vt_ready = LE_FALSE;

/* After the classic skin paints the button (background, border, text), smooth its
 * rounded corners. Fill matches the skin (pressed → BACKGROUND, released → BASE);
 * a LINE border is a 1px ring in SHADOWDARK (the colour the classic line-border
 * draw uses), so the AA reproduces backdrop → border → fill at each corner. The
 * radius is whatever the button was given — AaCorners_Render handles any value. */
static void aa_paint(leButtonWidget* btn)
{
    s_orig_paint(btn);

    if (btn->widget.status.drawState == LE_WIDGET_DRAW_STATE_DONE &&
        btn->widget.style.cornerRadius > 0u)
    {
        leRect   rect;
        leColor  fill;
        leColor  border;
        uint32_t bw;

        btn->fn->rectToScreen(btn, &rect);

        fill = leScheme_GetRenderColor(btn->widget.scheme,
                                       (btn->state != LE_BUTTON_STATE_UP)
                                           ? LE_SCHM_BACKGROUND : LE_SCHM_BASE);

        bw     = (btn->widget.style.borderType == LE_WIDGET_BORDER_LINE) ? 1u : 0u;
        border = (bw != 0u) ? leScheme_GetRenderColor(btn->widget.scheme, LE_SCHM_SHADOWDARK)
                            : fill;

        AaCorners_Render(&rect, btn->widget.style.cornerRadius, bw,
                         fill, border, leRenderer_CurrentColorMode());
    }
}

void ButtonAA_Enable(leButtonWidget* btn)
{
    if (!s_vt_ready)
    {
        s_aa_vt = *btn->fn;
        s_orig_paint = btn->fn->_paint;
        s_aa_vt._paint = aa_paint;
        s_vt_ready = LE_TRUE;
    }

    btn->fn = &s_aa_vt;
    btn->widget.fn = (const leWidgetVTable*)&s_aa_vt;
}

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-30 01:56:00Z)**_

Got it — you're right, I had the hierarchy wrong: the **canvas is the layer surface (OVR2)**, and `Marvin_PANEL_SONG_SELECT` is a **child widget** of the layer's root (`root2`), not the layer itself. So the panel is a normal widget I can round like a button.

But there's a real wrinkle that makes the top-level panel different from the buttons, and it's worth nailing before I code: **the AA corner needs something to reveal in the notch.** For a button, the notch reveals the opaque panel behind it. For the dialog's *outer* panel, the notch needs to reveal the **dashboard** (the floating-card look) — and OVR2 is currently **opaque RGB565**, so there's nothing to reveal; the corner would just blend the panel color against itself (no visible rounding).

To make the dialog read as a rounded card over the dashboard, OVR2 has to be **non-opaque at the corners**. The clean way:
- Dialog canvas → **RGBA8888**, AA writes **per-pixel alpha** (alpha 0 outside the arc, partial in the AA band, 255 inside), and OVR2 is configured for **per-pixel-alpha blending** so the dashboard composites through the corners, smoothly AA'd.

That's a bit of plumbing: the dialog canvas format change (1.45 MB → 2.9 MB), an alpha-writing mode in `aa_corners`, and enabling the OVR2 alpha blender. The alternative (RGB565 + chroma-key the corner color transparent) avoids the memory cost but gives a hard, non-AA'd key edge — defeats the point.

So before I build: do you want the **true rounded card** (dashboard visible through the corners → the RGBA8888 + per-pixel-alpha route), which is the only thing that makes rounding the *outer* panel look right? Or did you have a different intent for what shows in the corner — e.g., rounding an *inner* frame against a solid dialog backdrop instead of the outer edge?

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-30 02:05:03Z)**_

Real concern — the LCDC scans the layer out of DDR every frame regardless of whether it changed, so RGBA8888 doubles that region's *continuous* read bandwidth. Here's the math and the angles:

## The number
OVR2 covers just the dialog (1100×660 = 726 K px), not the full screen. RGB565→RGBA8888 adds 2 bytes/px:
- **~+87 MB/s @ 60 Hz** of extra DDR read (726K × 2 × 60), bounded to the dialog region.

## The decisive mitigation: it's only paid while the dialog is *open*
The dialog is a modal. Closed → OVR2 disabled → **zero** cost. So this never touches the **gameplay/capture** phase — it lands only during song-select, which is an idle menu moment. That alone makes it much less scary than a steady-state +87 MB/s.

## So the real question is: is the camera/vision pipeline live behind the dialog?
That's what decides whether +87 MB/s even matters:
- If song-select shows over a **dimmed/frozen** dashboard with the HEO camera + ISC paused → DDR has tons of headroom, RGBA8888 is a non-issue.
- If the **live video keeps running** behind it (HEO BGRX32 scanout + ISC capture write is already ~hundreds of MB/s on a ~16-bit DDR3 part), then +87 MB/s is a meaningful ~10-15% on an already-busy bus.

## A zero-bandwidth alternative, if you want it
Keep the dialog **RGB565/opaque** and **bake** the AA corners: sample the dashboard (BASE canvas) pixels behind each corner, blend the dialog edge over them, write the composite into the dialog's own RGB565 buffer. You get AA'd "see-through" corners with **no extra scanout bandwidth**. Trade-offs: the corner is a *static snapshot* (re-baked when the dialog repaints) — perfect if the dashboard behind is **dimmed/frozen** (which you'd mentioned wanting anyway), slightly stale if it's live; and it couples `aa_corners` to the dashboard buffer (pass it an explicit backdrop sampler instead of reading its own canvas).

## My recommendation
- If you're going to **dim/freeze the dashboard** behind the modal anyway → the **bake** approach is the elegant win: full AA card look, *zero* bandwidth cost, and staleness is a non-issue against a frozen backdrop.
- If the dashboard stays fully **live** behind it and you don't want the cross-layer coupling → **RGBA8888** is simplest and the cost is transient/menu-only — I wouldn't lose sleep over it.

Given you already floated dimming the base layer under the modal, I'd lean **bake** — it makes your bandwidth worry vanish and the dimmed backdrop is exactly the condition that makes baking look perfect. Want me to prototype that path (extend `AaCorners_Render` to take a backdrop sampler, feed it the dimmed dashboard), or just go RGBA8888?

```c
#include "ui/widgets/panel_aa/widget_panel_aa.h"

#include "ui/gfx/aa_corners.h"

#include "gfx/legato/core/legato_scheme.h"
#include "gfx/legato/renderer/legato_renderer.h"
#include "gfx/legato/widget/legato_widget.h"

/* One shared vtable copy + the captured original paint. Plain panels all share the
 * base leWidget vtable, so a single overridden copy serves every caller. */
static leWidgetVTable s_aa_vt;
static void (*s_orig_paint)(leWidget*);
static leBool s_vt_ready = LE_FALSE;

/* After the classic skin paints the panel (background fill + optional border),
 * smooth its rounded corners: fill is the panel's BASE colour, a LINE border is a
 * 1px SHADOWDARK ring. Backdrop is sampled from the panel's own corner pixel — the
 * opaque parent behind it. */
static void aa_paint(leWidget* wgt)
{
    s_orig_paint(wgt);

    if (wgt->status.drawState == LE_WIDGET_DRAW_STATE_DONE &&
        wgt->style.cornerRadius > 0u)
    {
        leRect   rect;
        leColor  fill;
        leColor  border;
        uint32_t bw;

        wgt->fn->rectToScreen(wgt, &rect);

        fill   = leScheme_GetRenderColor(wgt->scheme, LE_SCHM_BASE);
        bw     = (wgt->style.borderType == LE_WIDGET_BORDER_LINE) ? 1u : 0u;
        border = (bw != 0u) ? leScheme_GetRenderColor(wgt->scheme, LE_SCHM_SHADOWDARK)
                            : fill;

        AaCorners_Render(&rect, wgt->style.cornerRadius, bw,
                         fill, border, leRenderer_CurrentColorMode());
    }
}

void PanelAA_Enable(leWidget* panel)
{
    if (!s_vt_ready)
    {
        s_aa_vt = *panel->fn;
        s_orig_paint = panel->fn->_paint;
        s_aa_vt._paint = aa_paint;
        s_vt_ready = LE_TRUE;
    }

    panel->fn = &s_aa_vt;
}

```

Flash and check:

**One caveat to watch — catalog/SD timing.** `ScreenSongSelect_Setup` runs during boot (phase 2), and the song count is fixed at `Catalog_Count()` at that moment. The SD mounts asynchronously (services start at splash-shown, the dialog builds right after), so if the mount hasn't finished, the list will be **empty** (count latched at 0) even though the catalog loads moments later. So:
- If it's **populated** → SD was ready in time, we're good.
- If it's **empty** → it's this timing, not a logic bug. The fix is to re-set the model once the catalog is loaded — cleanest when we wire dialog **open/close** (reload-on-open), or I can add a small `ScreenSongSelect_RefreshCatalog()` the app calls after SD mount.

The clean fix is just **reload the model when the dialog opens** — a single `SongList_SetModel(list, Catalog_Count(), …)` call in the open path. No refresh subsystem; it falls out naturally when we wire open/close.

**Empty state — one caveat with the "label behind, covered by the list" plan:** the list widget paints its own area, so an MGS label placed *behind* it gets covered (that's literally the black you're seeing — the list over the dialog background). So the label-behind approach only works if the empty list is **transparent** (doesn't fill its background). 

I'd actually recommend the empty state live **inside the SongList widget** — draw a centered placeholder string (e.g. "No songs" / "Loading…") when `count == 0`. It's self-contained, reusable for any future list, and sidesteps the cover-up problem entirely. _**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-30 02:42:32Z)**_

Good questions, and they're related. Quick answer on coloring: **the SongList applies colors directly — hardcoded `SL_*` RGB888 constants** (`SL_BG 0x0E0E0E`, `SL_TITLE`, `SL_ARTIST`, …) converted to the layer mode at paint time. It does **not** read them from a scheme. The one place the scheme is consulted is the **glyph anti-alias lookup table** (`draw_str` blends text against the scheme's `BASE`) — so the scheme affects only how text edges AA, not the fill or text colors. The opaque dark rect you see is the hardcoded `SL_BG` fill (the widget even declares itself `BACKGROUND_FILL`/opaque on purpose).

So to make it "take its background from the panel," the move is to **not fill** and declare it transparent. Let me check what's actually behind the list (the LEFT panel's color) so the text AA blends against the right backdrop:
